sentences.pattern: I find it easier to concentrate on + printed or digital material + when + clause.
sentences.cn: 当……时，我发现更容易专注于某类阅读材料。
sentences.example: I find it easier to concentrate on printed books when I read before bed.

sentences.pattern: The kind of book I am most likely to choose is + genre + because + clause.
sentences.cn: 我最可能选择的书籍类型是……，因为……
sentences.example: The kind of book I am most likely to choose is biography because I enjoy real experiences.

sentences.pattern: Regular reading exposes people not only to + noun, but also to + noun.
sentences.cn: 规律阅读不仅让人接触……，也让人接触……
sentences.example: Regular reading exposes people not only to new vocabulary, but also to unfamiliar viewpoints.

The plot is simple, but the novel is a real page-turner.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Reading for pleasure supports academic development.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Voluntary reading can strengthen language and thinking skills without feeling like formal study.
writingIdeas.argument: Readers meet words repeatedly in meaningful contexts, which helps vocabulary become usable rather than merely recognised. Longer texts also require them to remember earlier information and follow an argument or plot. These habits support concentration in subjects beyond language learning. Because the reader chooses the material, motivation may be stronger than during compulsory exercises. Schools should therefore make appealing books available as well as teaching examination skills.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Digital reading is convenient but can encourage fragmented attention.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: The device used for reading may influence how consistently a reader remains with a text.
writingIdeas.argument: A phone or tablet gives immediate access to books, articles and dictionaries. The same device, however, also contains messages, videos and alerts that invite the reader to switch tasks. Frequent interruption makes it harder to maintain the argument of a demanding text. Readers can reduce this problem by disabling notifications or using a dedicated e-reader. The issue is not that screens prevent comprehension, but that digital environments often compete for attention.

speaking.question: How often do you read books or long articles?
speaking.answer: I read something substantial most days, usually for half an hour before bed. During the week it’s often a novel because I want a break from work-related material. At weekends I’m more likely to read a long newspaper article or biography. I’m not a very fast reader, but I’m fairly consistent, which matters more to me.

speaking.question: Do you prefer printed books or e-books?
speaking.answer: For novels, I still prefer a printed copy. I like seeing how far I’ve progressed, and there are no notifications to distract me. E-books are more practical when I’m travelling, though, because I can carry several without adding weight. So my preference really depends on where I’m reading rather than a strong dislike of screens.

reading.title: Why Deep Reading Takes Time
paragraphs: Reading appears instantaneous because skilled readers recognise many words without conscious effort. Understanding a demanding text, however, involves several slower processes. A reader connects a sentence with earlier information, decides which details matter and sometimes revises an interpretation after reaching a later paragraph. Deep reading is therefore not simply the rapid movement of the eyes across a page.

Experiments on comprehension often distinguish between locating information and building a mental model. A person can scan a timetable for a departure time without understanding the document as a whole. By contrast, following an argument requires the reader to hold claims in memory and recognise relationships such as cause, contrast and qualification. Speed is useful only if these connections survive it.

Digital formats have complicated the picture. Search functions and links make reference faster, while adjustable text benefits readers with visual difficulties. Yet scrolling can make the physical location of information less memorable, and connected devices offer easy routes away from the text. Researchers have not concluded that one medium is always superior. Task, device design and reading habits all influence the result.

The desire to read faster is understandable when information is abundant. Nevertheless, efficiency sometimes means choosing a suitable pace rather than maximising words per minute. A report may deserve close annotation; a familiar news story may require only a quick scan. Skilled readers vary their method according to purpose. In this view, slow reading is not evidence of weakness when the material demands reflection—it is one of several strategies available to an experienced reader.

Deep reading is also affected by prior knowledge. A specialist can process a difficult article quickly because many concepts are already organised in memory; a newcomer must pause to build those connections. Comparing their speed without considering background is misleading. Fluency develops partly through reading widely enough for common structures and ideas to become familiar.
